title: Gavin Newsom Just Did Something Incredibly Important
text:
Supported by
Guest Essay
The Twisted Logic of the Death Penalty Is Losing Its Power
The death penalty in America is not about whether people deserve to die for the crimes they commit; it is about whether our imperfect governments deserve to kill. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation last week of all of California’s 548 death sentences to life imprisonment without parole is a remarkable act of moral leadership.
California’s death penalty has cost taxpayers billions of dollars. It has absorbed enormous judicial and legal resources, even though California’s homicide rate has dropped dramatically without a single execution in 20 years. No one disputes that people on California’s death row have been convicted of horrific crimes. Many law enforcement officials and survivors of victims have understandably expressed anger about these commutations. My grandfather was murdered when I was 16, and I understand the rage and pain that violent crime produces. But we must reject the policy of blood for blood. The men and women who were on California’s death row will still be severely punished without the death penalty.
The U.S. Supreme Court effectively ended capital punishment in 1972 when it concluded in Furman v. Georgia that the death penalty had been applied in an arbitrary and unreliable manner, violating the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment.
In many states, particularly former Confederate states in the South, the disproportionate execution of Black and poor people was considered so essential that new discretionary schemes for imposing the death penalty were quickly devised. Within four years, the Supreme Court upheld a new era of capital punishment that spread across the nation.
The modern death penalty has been a complete failure. It is characterized by wrongful convictions, racial bias, unreliable proceedings and arbitrary and unjust sentencing. More than 200 people sentenced to death have been exonerated of the crimes for which they were convicted. For every eight people executed in America, one innocent person has been identified. This astonishing failure ratio would never be tolerated in aviation, food safety or virtually any other area of public policy — but executions persist.
Recent executions have exposed the cruelty of capital punishment in graphic and shocking ways. Botched executions, where condemned people writhe, gasp for air, moan and struggle before death, have become common in multiple states. The recent, torturous execution attempt in Tennessee that left Christa Pike unconscious for days forced many Americans to confront the myth that lethal injection leads to a peaceful death.
